message.content:
### Tenant Rights in Texas (as of 2024) | Area | What You’re Entitled To | Key Points | |------|------------------------|------------| | **Security Deposit** | • Must be returned within 30 days after you move out (unless you and the landlord agree otherwise).
• Landlord may keep money only for unpaid rent, damages beyond normal wear‑and‑tear, or other costs specified in the lease. | • Landlord must give a written itemized list of deductions.
• If the landlord fails to return the deposit or provide an itemized statement, you can sue for the full amount plus damages. | | **Habitability** | • Landlord must maintain the premises in a safe, sanitary condition.
• Repairs for structural issues, plumbing, heating, electrical, and pest control must be made promptly. | • Texas Property Code §92.001 requires landlords to keep premises in good repair.
• If repairs are not made, you may withhold rent, repair and deduct, or terminate the lease (see §92.002). | | **Lease Terms** | • Written lease must include:
 • Name of landlord and tenant(s)
 • Address of rental unit
 • Amount of rent and due date
 • Security deposit amount
 • Lease duration
 • Rules for pets, smoking, etc. | • Oral leases are enforceable but harder to prove.
• Landlord cannot add new terms after the lease is signed without your consent. | | **Rent Increases** | • For month‑to‑month leases, rent can be increased at any time, but you must receive written notice at least 30 days before the increase takes effect.
• For fixed‑term leases, rent can only be increased at the start of a new term unless the lease allows it. | • Notice must be in writing and specify the new amount and effective date. | | **Eviction Process** | • Landlord must provide a written notice:
 • 3‑day notice to pay rent or vacate (for nonpayment).
 • 30‑day notice to vacate (for lease violations).
 • 60‑day notice to vacate (for no‑cause termination of month‑to‑month lease). | • After notice, landlord files a lawsuit in district court.
• Tenants have the right to contest the eviction in court. | | **Right to Quiet Enjoyment** | • You have the right to live in the unit without unreasonable interference from the landlord or other tenants. | • Landlord may not enter the unit except for emergencies, repairs, inspections (with 24‑hour notice), or to show the unit to prospective renters (with 24‑hour notice). | | **Discrimination Protections** | • Landlords cannot discriminate based on race, color, religion, sex, national origin, familial status, disability, or source of income (e.g., public assistance). | • These protections are enforced under the Texas Fair Housing Act and the federal Fair Housing Act. | | **Pet Policies** | • Landlord may require a pet deposit or fee, but cannot charge more than $200 for a pet deposit. | • Landlord can’t refuse a pet if the lease already allows pets, unless the pet causes damage or violates local ordinances. | | **Utilities** | • Landlord must provide water, heat, and electricity unless the lease specifies otherwise. | • If utilities are included, the landlord must keep them in working order. | | **Repair and Deduct** | • If the landlord fails to make necessary repairs, you may repair the issue yourself and deduct the cost from your rent (up to the amount of the rent). | • You must provide receipts and notify the landlord in writing. | | **Right to Access Records** | • You can request copies of the lease, security deposit receipts, and any notices sent by the landlord. | • Landlord must provide these documents upon reasonable request. | --- #### How to Exercise Your Rights 1. **Document Everything** - Keep copies of all communications (emails, texts, letters). - Take photos or videos of any maintenance issues. 2. **Written Notices** - Send notices via certified mail or email with read receipt to establish proof of delivery. 3. **Repair and Deduct** - If you choose this route, keep receipts and send a written notice to the landlord before making the repair. 4. **Legal Action** - If the landlord violates your rights, you can file a claim in district court. - Small claims court (up to $20,000) is often used for disputes over deposits or minor damages. 5. **Seek Mediation** - Many counties offer free or low‑cost mediation services for landlord‑tenant disputes. --- #### Resources | Resource | What It Offers | How to Access | |----------|----------------|---------------| | **Texas Attorney General – Consumer Protection Division** | Information on tenant rights, dispute resolution, and consumer complaints. | https://www.texasattorneygeneral.gov/consumer-protection | | **Texas Department of Housing and Community Affairs (TDHCA)** | Fair housing guidance, landlord‑tenant laws, and complaint filing. | https://www.tdhca.state.tx.us/ | | **Local County Clerk’s Office** | Filing small claims, eviction filings, and court procedures. | Visit your county clerk’s website or office. | | **Legal Aid Organizations** | Free or low‑cost legal representation for qualifying tenants. | Search “legal aid Texas” or visit https://www.lawhelp.org/ | | **Texas Landlord‑Tenant Law Summary** | Quick reference guide to key statutes. | https://www.texasattorneygeneral.gov/sites/default/files/2024-01/Texas%20Landlord-Tenant%20Law%20Summary.pdf | --- #### Quick Checklist Before Moving In - [ ] Read the lease thoroughly; ask questions about any unclear clauses. - [ ] Verify the landlord’s identity and ownership of the property. - [ ] Request a copy of the security deposit receipt and itemized list of any fees. - [ ] Confirm the landlord’s responsibilities for repairs and maintenance. - [ ] Check local ordinances for any additional tenant protections (e.g., rent control, eviction moratoriums). --- ### Bottom Line In Texas, tenants enjoy a solid set of statutory protections covering security deposits, habitability, notice requirements, and anti‑discrimination. While the state does not impose rent caps, it does require landlords to maintain safe, livable premises and to follow proper eviction procedures. If you believe your landlord is violating your rights, you have several avenues—repair and deduct, written notices, mediation, or court action—to protect yourself. Always keep records and seek professional advice when needed.
